extracted.intended_audience: scientists and students of scientific method; readers interested in philosophy and practice of physical science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for using, evaluating, and improving approximate laws, measurements, and models in physical science. Emphasizes when idealizations are appropriate, how to recognise and account for errors, and how to proceed by successive approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat idealized constructs as hypothetical approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: All then is merely approximate. We speak and calculate about inflexible bars, inextensible lines, heavy points, homogeneous substances, uniform spheres, perfect fluids and gases, and we deduce a great number of beautiful theorems; but all is hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ideal objects (inflexible bars, perfect spheres, perfect gases, straight lines, etc.) are conveniences for calculation, not literal realities; explicitly acknowledge which idealizations are assumed and consider their physical implications (e.g., bending, inhomogeneity, thermodynamic effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for instrument limitations and measurement faults
rubrics_metrics.description: All the instruments with which we perform our measurements are faulty. We assume that a plumb-line gives a vertical line; but this is never true in an absolute sense ... the pendulum is not theoretically perfect, except for infinitely small arcs of vibration, and the delicate experiments performed with the torsion balance proceed on the assumption that the force of torsion of a wire is proportional to the angle of torsion, which again is only true for infinitely small angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and correct for known deviations of instruments (e.g., plumb-line divergence due to local mass, mercury surface deviations, pendulum non-isochronism, torsion balance linearity limits); in accurate surveys determine and allow for such divergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical methods when they give truer results
rubrics_metrics.description: Such is the purely approximate character of all our operations that it is not uncommon to find the theoretically worse method giving truer results than the theoretically perfect method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose methods based on practical performance and feasibility, not merely theoretical optimality (examples: cycloidal pendulum vs common pendulum; spherical mirrors vs true parabola when difference is negligible and manufacture easier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish laws believed to be exact from those only approximate
rubrics_metrics.description: We must accordingly draw a strong distinction between the laws of nature which we believe to be accurately stated in our formulas, and those to which our statements only make an approximation, so that at a future time the law will be differently stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly categorize theoretical statements as (a) likely exact laws (e.g., law of gravitation as commonly stated) versus (b) empirical formulas subject to modification (e.g., latent heat relationships), and treat them differently in inference and expectation of future revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a probable precise law over approximate numerical results when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind may seem to pass in advance of its data, and choose out certain numerical results as absolutely true. We can never really pass beyond our data, and so far as assumption enters in, so far want of certainty will attach to our conclusions; nevertheless we may sometimes rightly prefer a probable assumption of a precise law to numerical results, which are at the best only approximate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimental numbers are noisy, it can be justifiable to assume a simple exact law if repeated evidence and theoretical considerations support it — but note the assumption and its uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use successive approximations: start simple then refine
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific problems, one generation is usually able to make some bold hypothetical simplification, upon which the next investigator makes hypothetical modifications approaching more nearly to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an iterative approach: make initial simplifying hypotheses to obtain tractable results (e.g., Newton's spherical hypothesis), then introduce successive corrections (e.g., spheroidal terms, perturbations) as understanding and methods improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to hidden or undetectable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: No phenomenon comes within the sphere of our senses unless it possesses a momentum capable of irritating the appropriate nerves. There may then be worlds of phenomena too slight to rise within the scope of our consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the possibility of undetected effects below current detection thresholds; consider whether unexplained residuals might indicate such phenomena and invest in more sensitive tests when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and test neglected terms and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove, then, the difficulties in the way of the undulatory theory of light, a new approach to probable conditions was needed. Cauchy was able to make a new approximation under the more difficult supposition ... To calculate the rate of propagation of disturbance in such a medium is a work of excessive difficulty. The complete solution of the problem appears indeed to be beyond human power, so that we must be content ... to look forward to successive approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a theory makes simplifying assumptions, identify the neglected quantities and evaluate when they become significant; rework the approximation under more realistic suppositions (example: spacing of particles in wave theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical incompleteness from incorrect physical law
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to distinguish between those problems which are physically and those which are merely mathematically incomplete. In the latter case the physical law is correctly seized, but the mathematician neglects, or is more often unable to follow out the law in all its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discrepancies arise, consider whether they stem from incomplete mathematical development (e.g., not summing infinite reflections) rather than from failure of the underlying physical law (example: Young's rings and Poisson's resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use idealized limit models (perfect gas, perfect bodies) as useful but unattainable references
rubrics_metrics.description: In some branches of science we meet with natural laws of a simple character which are in a certain point of view exactly true and yet can never be manifested as exactly true in natural phenomena. Such, for instance, are the laws concerning what is called a perfect gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ idealized models (perfect gas, perfect centrobaric body, etc.) as conceptual limits to guide reasoning, but explicitly state their domain of applicability and the nature of departures in real systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base truncation of series/terms on variable scale and measurement resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If y be a function of x then we may say that y = A + Bx + Cx^2 + D x^3 + ... When x is made small enough the quantity y seems to obey the equation y = A + Bx. If X should be still less ... y would appear to be the fixed quantity A ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which powers/terms to retain in expansions by considering the magnitude of the variable relative to measurement sensitivity and the size of coefficients; explicitly justify neglecting higher-order terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin modelling with simplest (linear) laws and increase complexity only as indicated
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a general rule in quantitative investigation that we commence by discovering linear, and afterwards proceed to elliptic or more complicated laws of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model locally with lowest-order variation (linear), and progress to quadratic, cubic, etc., only when residuals or theoretical considerations require; use the classification linear/elliptic/cubic to communicate model order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance theoretical exactness against manufacturability/practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: The spherical form is not the correct form for a speculum or lense, but it differs so slightly from the true form, and is so much more easily produced mechanically, that it is generally best to rest content with the spherical surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the theoretical optimum is costly or impractical and the deviation is negligible for purposes, prefer practical approximations; document the trade-off and quantify the error magnitude where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and correct for all relevant experimental error sources
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot accurately perform the simple experiment of compressing gas in a bent tube by a column of mercury ... without paying regard to — (1) the variations of atmospheric pressure, which are communicated to the gas through the mercury; (2) the compressibility of mercury; (3) the temperature of the mercury; (4) the temperature of the gas; (5) the expansion of the glass tube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before claiming experimental confirmation, enumerate and, where possible, quantify all sources of error and systematic bias; consider environmental, material, and apparatus effects and correct for them (example list above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulate repeated experimental tests before assuming completeness of a law
rubrics_metrics.description: Only as repeated doubts have time after time been resolved in favour of the law of Newton, has it been assumed as precisely correct. But this belief does not rest on experiment or observation only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a law as provisionally precise only after repeated testing and resolution of alternate explanations; note both experimental confirmation and theoretical grounds for confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical reasoning/analogy to support expected law forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever influence spreads from a point, and expands uniformly through space, will doubtless vary inversely in intensity as the square of the distance, because the area over which it is spread increases as the square of the radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing functional forms (e.g., inverse-square), use geometric or physical arguments (conservation over area, analogy with other emanating forces) as independent support for the proposed law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat solutions as provisional and open to minor residual corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are successively pointed out in previous investigations ... a series of minor inaccuracies remain to be corrected and explained, were our powers of reasoning sufficiently great, and the purpose adequate in importance!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present results as successive approximations with acknowledged residuals; prioritize corrections based on their magnitude and importance relative to the purpose of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model local curve behaviour with appropriate polynomial order depending on arc length
rubrics_metrics.description: If we take any curve and regard a portion of it free from any kind of discontinuity, we may represent the character of such portion by an equation ... Restrict the attention to a very small portion of the curve, and the eye will be unable to distinguish its difference from a straight line ... Take a larger portion ... it will be possible to draw a parabola or ellipse so that the curve shall apparently coincide ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate curve segments by straight lines or low-degree polynomials for small arcs; expand polynomial order as the domain examined grows until residuals vanish.
